title: LMML – Live Museum of Movie Locations
subtitle: A one-day visit to fifteen London filming locations
author: Claudia Briccolani

cover.intro:
LMML treats London as a museum whose rooms are streets. Its fifteen exhibits are places where a film or a television series was shot between 1964 and 2019: the station where the Beatles run from their fans in A Hard Day's Night, the blue door of Notting Hill, the mews, the chapel and the department store of Love Actually, the market and the bridge of the Harry Potter films, the front door, the park bench and the hospital roof of Sherlock, the café and the restaurant of Fleabag.

This site is the companion to the visit. Each location has its own page, with photographs, a table of data about the place and the scene, and a text; a QR code posted at the location opens the same page on your phone. The map shows every stop, the route of the day and the estimated position and direction of the camera.

Two narratives. The places can be visited in two different orders. Historical timeline follows the release dates of the works, decade by decade, and tells how London on screen has changed; it visits fourteen of the fifteen places. Recreate the shot follows the map, visits all fifteen and is for visitors who want to stand where the camera stood: it adds, at every stop, where to stand, how the light falls and what to look for. Choose one below; you can switch at any time from the menu, and the Previous and Next buttons will follow the narrative you chose.

Texts that adapt to you. On every location page six buttons change the text: Tell me more / Tell me less for the length, Too simple / Too difficult for the level, Do you want to play? / Additional details and references for the tone. A button is disabled when there is no text in that direction. A short French version is available where you see the Français button.

Camera positions are estimates and the information is still being verified: pages say so until each location has been checked on site.

disclaimer.title: Disclaimer
disclaimer.template:
The purpose of this web site is to explore various types of typographic and layout style for specialized tourist visits, as an end-of-course project for the 'Information Modeling and Web technologies' course of the Master's Degree in Digital Humanities and Digital Knowledge of the University of Bologna, under the supervision of prof. Fabio Vitali.

docs.title: Design choices
docs.text:
[DRAFT – review] The app is a companion for a visitor walking in the street with a phone, so it is designed mobile-first. Content lives in JSON and presentation in CSS: a declarative approach, as the course emphasises active documents over procedural code. The same data must work with any theme and any narrative.

The site is a single HTML page (index.html) that loads one stylesheet for structure (css/base.css), one stylesheet per theme (css/themes/), three JSON data files (data/) and JavaScript ES modules (js/). There is no framework, no build step and no npm dependency. Two libraries are loaded from cdnjs.cloudflare.com: Leaflet 1.9.4 for the map, with OpenStreetMap tiles, and qrcodejs 1.0.0 for the QR codes.

Sections 1.1 to 1.3 describe the canvas, the HTML vocabulary and the layouts of the location page. Section 5 describes how the code is organised.

sections.title: Viewport-sized canvas and scroll containers
sections.text:
[DRAFT – review] It is a requirement of the assignment: “The canvas should be exactly as big as the viewport. Individual texts and metadata viewer will scroll in their own containers within the canvas.” (Course slides, “Warnings”).

The html element has height: 100% and overflow: hidden. The body has height: 100vh, then 100dvh for browsers that support it, and overflow: hidden. The body is a grid whose areas and rows come from two custom properties: --app-areas (default "header" "main" "footer") and --app-rows (default auto minmax(0, 1fr) auto). The main element has min-height: 0 and overflow: hidden.

Scrolling happens only in these containers:

  • elements with the attribute data-scroll (overflow: auto, min-height: 0, overscroll-behavior: contain): the body of every text page (page-body), the text of a location (text-body) and the metadata block (location-meta) in the wide layout;
  • the image strip of a location (location-media), which scrolls sideways with scroll snapping;
  • the opened directions (transition-text), limited to min(40dvh, 16rem);
  • in the narrow layout, the content wrapper of the location page (location-content), which is then the only vertical scroll container of that page;
  • in the wide layout, the location article itself (overflow-y: auto), used only if the rows of a theme do not fit;
  • the site header while the phone menu is open (max-height: 70dvh);
  • the Leaflet map, which pans inside its own box.

For printing, a media query sets height: auto and overflow: visible on html, body, main, the page article and the data-scroll containers, and hides the header, the footer and the print button.

TODO (rewrite): Found with screenshots at 390×844, 844×390 and 1280×800 on 2026-10-06: on phones the location text was not visible at all. The chain from main to the text container already had min-height: 0 at every level; the cause was the grid of the article, whose header row was auto and held the full directions text. An auto row is sized to its content before the flexible rows share what is left, so a long header left nothing for the rows below, and main, with overflow: hidden, clipped them with no way to scroll. The fix bounds every auto row (the directions are closed by default and scroll when open; the toolbar is one row) and gives the article itself overflow-y: auto as a last resort.

Measured before the fix on the location pages, in both themes: at 390×844 the text container had a height of 0 px; at 844×390 it was 47–50 px high and lay entirely below the visible part of main; 44 controls were out of reach and 20 partly cut off. After the fix the same pages show no clipped or unreachable control. The measurements are in screenshots/REPORT.md, which is not part of the published site.

sections.title: HTML vocabulary and style hooks
sections.text:
[DRAFT – review] The assignment says that the HTML vocabulary can, and probably should, be restricted, and to use special classes or data-* attributes. The data-role hooks let each theme restyle and rearrange everything without changing the HTML, which is what makes themes switchable.

The lists below were extracted from index.html, the scripts in js/ and the HTML strings in data/ as they are now.

Elements in index.html (21): a, body, button, div, footer, head, header, html, label, li, link, main, meta, nav, noscript, p, script, select, span, title, ul.

Elements created by the scripts (26): a, article, button, caption, details, div, figcaption, figure, h1, h2, h3, header, img, li, nav, ol, p, section, span, summary, table, tbody, td, th, tr, ul.

Elements inside the HTML texts of the data files (location texts, transitions, chapter and narrative texts, cover, disclaimer): a, em, h3, li, ol, p, strong. The documentation texts also use table, tbody, tr, th, td, ul and div.

Classes. The site's own HTML has no class attribute. Classes are used only on the shapes Leaflet draws on the map: lmml-marker, lmml-marker--in-route, lmml-route, lmml-camera-cone, lmml-camera-arrow, lmml-camera and lmml-tooltip. base.css also addresses one Leaflet class, .leaflet-bar a, to enlarge the zoom buttons.

Identifiers. theme-css (the theme stylesheet link), site-menu and site-switchers (referenced by aria-controls of the menu button), and docs-N-N on every documentation section.

ARIA and related attributes: aria-controls, aria-current, aria-disabled, aria-expanded, aria-hidden, aria-label, aria-pressed; role="group" on the switch groups; title on the text switches and the map link; lang on the text container and the language buttons; hidden on the links of the previous / next bar; rel and target on external links; scope on table headers; loading="lazy" on images.

sections.title: Portrait and landscape layouts
sections.text:
[DRAFT – review] On a phone the visitor needs, in order, to recognise the place (title, work, picture), to read about it, and to change the text. Directions are needed while walking, not after arriving, so they are collapsed behind a one-line summary. All switches must be visible without scrolling, because changing the text is a core requirement and hidden controls would not be discovered.

TODO (rewrite in my own words, with the reasons): The location page has three layouts, selected by media queries in css/base.css. It is wide when the viewport is in landscape, wider than 600px and taller than 500px. Otherwise it is narrow: in portrait, or at most 600px wide, or at most 500px high. A narrow viewport at most 500px high (a phone in landscape) is also short. The section title still says portrait and landscape; these are the conditions actually used.

LayoutGrid areas of the article (default)Rows (default)Variables a theme can redefine
Wide"header header" / "media text" / "meta text" / "qr text", columns minmax(0, 2fr) minmax(0, 3fr)auto / minmax(calc(var(--loc-image-min) + 3.5rem), 1.4fr) / minmax(0, 1fr) / auto--loc-landscape-areas, -columns, -rows
Narrow"header" / "tabs" / "content" / "toolbar", one columnauto / auto / minmax(0, 1fr) / auto--loc-narrow-areas, -columns, -rows
Short"header header" / "content content" / "tabs toolbar", columns auto minmax(0, 1fr)auto / minmax(0, 1fr) / auto--loc-short-areas, -columns, -rows

The DOM of a location page is the same in the three layouts: an article containing the header, the tabs (Text, Info, QR code), a wrapper (location-content) around the image strip and the three panels (text, metadata, QR code), and a toolbar. In the wide layout the wrapper has display: contents, so the image strip and the panels are grid items of the article; the tabs and the toolbar are not displayed and all panels are visible. In the narrow layout the wrapper is a block with overflow-y: auto and holds the image strip and the one panel selected by the tabs.

TODO (rewrite): In the narrow layout the header shows the title, then one line with the work, the flag 'Not verified' and the directions line. A location that is not a step of the current narrative has one more line: the note 'Not part of “(name of the narrative)”.' and the link 'Return to the narrative', which is 44px high. On such a page the previous / next bar of the shell is not displayed in the narrow layout: it would contain only the same link. The chapter line is not displayed in the narrow layout. In the wide layout the header shows the directions line, the chapter line, the title, the work and 'Information not yet verified'; the note reads 'This location is not part of the narrative “…”. It is part of: …' followed by the same link, and the bar of the shell keeps its own 'Return to the narrative'.

[DRAFT – review] The chapter line is hidden on phones for reasons of space; the chapter is introduced by its own chapter screen before its first location.

TODO (rewrite): The toolbar of the narrow layout does not scroll. The six text switches are grouped by axis into three pairs, each under the name of its axis: Length (More, Less), Level (Harder, Simpler), Tone (Play, Details). A fourth group, Language, holds the language buttons. At 390px wide the three pairs fill one row and a second row holds the language buttons and the link 'Show on the map'; in the short layout everything is on one row beside the tabs and the link reads 'Map'. The buttons show their short label in the toolbar and the wording of the assignment in the wide layout. The switch 'Too simple' moves to a higher level and its short label is 'Harder'; 'Too difficult' moves to a lower level and its short label is 'Simpler'. Every switch has the wording of the assignment as its title attribute, and an aria-label made of the short label and the wording, for example 'Harder: Too simple'. Measured at 390×844 in both themes: 9 controls, 2 rows, toolbar 123px high; at 844×390: 1 row, 60px high.

[DRAFT – review] A button label must say what the button does, not how the user feels: “Too simple” asks for a harder text, so it is labelled “Harder”. The full wording of the assignment is kept in the accessible name and in the tooltip.

TODO (rewrite): The text switches and the link to the map are the only elements that change parent. The function placeControls in js/render/location.js appends them to the toolbar when the media query (orientation: portrait), (max-width: 600px), (max-height: 500px) matches, and puts them back (switches first in the text panel, map link last in the QR block) when it does not; it runs when the page is rendered and on every change of that media query, and the listener is removed when the route changes. The same three conditions are written in section 11 of css/base.css. The directions to a location are a details element, closed when the page opens at every size. Its summary is built from the transition data: the minutes, then the Underground lines if the transition lists any, otherwise the mode; for example '36 min · Central + Piccadilly lines' or '13 min · Walk'. When opened, the directions are positioned over the page below the header (position: absolute) and scroll in a box limited to min(40dvh, 16rem).

TODO (rewrite): Two sizes are set in css/base.css with a lower limit that a theme cannot go below. Controls: --target-size, default 44px, applied as min-height and min-width max(44px, var(--target-size)) to button, select, summary, the site title, the links of the menu, the previous / next links, the map link, the links of the documentation contents and of the chapter lists, and Leaflet's zoom buttons; the 'Return to the narrative' link of the compact header has the same minimum. Picture: --loc-image-min-height, default 10rem; the value used is --loc-image-min = clamp(6rem, var(--loc-image-min-height), 35vh). It is the minimum height of the picture row of each figure and, plus 3.5rem, the minimum of the media row of the default wide layout. A theme that redefines --loc-landscape-rows replaces that minimum for the media row.

References for the target size: WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.5.5 Target Size (Enhanced), Level AAA: 'at least 44 by 44 CSS pixels' (W3C, Understanding SC 2.5.5); WCAG 2.2, Success Criterion 2.5.8 Target Size (Minimum), Level AA: 'at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels' (W3C, Understanding SC 2.5.8); Apple Human Interface Guidelines, Accessibility.

TODO (author): confirm the 44x44 pt figure on that page.

[DRAFT – review] The user is outdoors, often walking, using one hand. 24px is the WCAG 2.2 AA minimum (2.5.8); 44px is the WCAG 2.5.5 AAA target and Apple's recommendation.

Measured on the two reference pages after the changes: picture 160–177px high at 1280×800, 160px at 390×844, 104–137px at 844×390; no control smaller than 44×44px at the three sizes in both themes.

docs.title: Metadata model
docs.text:
[DRAFT – review] schema.org is a widely used shared vocabulary that already covers places, films, TV series and images (Uniform, from the RSTU properties in the slides). A separate namespace is used only for facts specific to filming locations that schema.org does not cover, so they are represented as they are, without forcing them into unsuitable terms (Tailored).

The content is in three JSON files. data/locations.json has an @context and a list of 15 locations; data/narratives.json has a list of 2 narratives; data/site.json has the texts of the site, the list of themes and this documentation. The files are plain JSON shaped like JSON-LD: the scripts read them with fetch and do not process the @context.

The @context of locations.json declares "@vocab": "https://schema.org/" and "lmml": "https://claudiabriccolani.github.io/web-tech-proj/ns#". Property names without a prefix are schema.org terms (section 2.1); names with the prefix lmml: are defined by this project (section 2.2). The page at that address, ns/index.html in the repository, lists every lmml: term with its definition; it reads the list from section 2.2 of this documentation when it is opened, and gives each term an identifier equal to its name without the prefix (for example ns#cameraBearing).

sections.title: The text grid (length × level × tone)
sections.text:
[DRAFT – review] The three axes come from the assignment's grid (length / competence / tone). The three cells written for each location cover the extremes and the middle (short · intro · young, medium · average · adult, long · advanced · scholar), so each target audience has a text and every switch has a direction to move in. Short texts also exist in French, for the use case of visitors from Brussels.

Every text has a position on three ordered axes and a language: length (short, medium, long), level (intro, average, advanced), tone (young, adult, scholar), language (inLanguage: en or fr). The grid has 27 cells per language. Only one text may occupy a cell in a language; the data check reports duplicates.

Each of the 15 locations has the same four texts: three in English and one in French. In the narrative Recreate the shot every step also has one English text in the cell medium · average · adult, which replaces the location's text of that cell while that narrative is selected (section 2.5). The Historical timeline has no step texts.

sections.title: Facts, sources and open questions
sections.text:
Every location carries the material its texts are written from. lmml:facts is a list of short statements, each with the address of the source it comes from (169 facts in all). Every such address must also be in the location's citation list (86 entries in all), which feeds the disclaimer page; the data check verifies this, and does the same for the sources of lmml:visitorAccess. lmml:openQuestions records points on which sources disagree or that could not be confirmed.

The metadata table of a location page is generated from the location object. It does not show lmml:facts, lmml:openQuestions, lmml:imageTodo and lmml:imageNote (nor identifier, image and lmml:texts, which are shown elsewhere on the page or not at all). It does show lmml:cameraConfidence, as 'Camera data', and lmml:visitorAccess, as 'Visiting and photography' with a source link per statement and the date checked. The open questions, the missing images and the points to verify are listed for the author in VERIFY.md, in the repository.

TODO: expand.

sections.title: Narrative texts and languages
sections.text:
A narrative step may carry its own lmml:texts. Such a text replaces the location's default text of the same cell and language, and only that one; the other texts of the location stay available. The text container records where the shown text comes from (data-text-source: location or narrative).

Texts have an inLanguage. When a location has texts in more than one language, one button per language is shown; the six switches then move among the texts of the current language only. The language chosen is remembered. If no text exists in the remembered language, all valid texts are used. All locations currently have English and French, with one French text each, so in French all six switches are disabled.

sections.text:

sections.title: Sources, images and licences
sections.text:
[DRAFT – review] Film stills are copyrighted by the producers, and the site must respect the copyright statement in the disclaimer required by the course. For two places no freely licensed photo exists, and the page says so.

Sources. Each location lists its sources in citation, as CreativeWork objects with url and description. Each fact (lmml:facts) and each visitor-access statement carries the address of one of those sources. The long text of every location ends with a list of references built from the sources of its facts.

Images. There are 27 images, all taken from Wikimedia Commons and stored in img/ as files at most 960px wide. Each has: contentUrl (the file), caption, lmml:alt, creditText (author, licence name, 'via Wikimedia Commons'), creator (the author as a Person), license (the address of the licence) and url (its page on Wikimedia Commons). Licences: 11 × CC BY-SA 2.0, 7 × CC BY-SA 4.0, 3 × CC BY 2.0, 3 × CC BY-SA 3.0, 2 × CC BY 4.0, 1 × CC0. No film still is used.

On the location page. Each image is shown with its alt attribute taken from lmml:alt (the caption is used only if lmml:alt is missing), its caption, and a credit line: 'Credit:' followed by creditText, a link 'License' to the licence and a link 'Source' to the Commons page.

On the disclaimer page. The list of sources is generated from the data: every citation and every image source page of every location, merged by address. Each entry shows the address, the description (for an image: 'Image', its caption and its creditText), a link 'Licence' when the entry is an image, and the names of the locations that use it. When the same page is both a cited source and the source page of an image, the entry keeps both descriptions. The disclaimer text is a template in site.json with three placeholders: the names of the source sites, the list, and the author.

Locations with no freely licensed photo of the exact place (searched on Wikimedia Commons by name and by position on 2026-10-06): Fleabag's café (20 York Rise): “No freely licensed photo of the café front at 20 York Rise was found: the picture shows the street, not the café.”; Smith & Wollensky (The Adelphi): “No freely licensed photo of the restaurant's own entrance or of its interior was found: the pictures show the building it is in.” The sentence is stored in lmml:imageNote and shown under the images of that location.

Captions. All images were opened and compared with their captions on 2026-10-06; ten captions were reworded to say only what the picture shows, and one (the blue door) is an open question. The record is in CAPTIONS.md, in the repository.

Checks. At startup the data check reports an image without license, without source url or without lmml:alt, and a fact or visitor-access statement whose source is not in citation.

Icon. favicon.svg, in the root of the site, is declared in index.html.

sections.title: How a theme overrides the layout
sections.text:
TODO

Mechanism, as implemented: a theme is a stylesheet in css/themes/ registered in the themes list of data/site.json (id, label, href). js/theme.js sets data-theme on the html element and changes the href of the link with id theme-css, so one theme stylesheet is loaded at a time. Theme rules are scoped with :root[data-theme="id"]. A theme changes the layout by redefining custom properties declared in section 1 of css/base.css:

  • all custom properties of base.css: --app-areas, --app-rows, --color-accent, --color-accent-contrast, --color-bg, --color-border, --color-fg, --color-muted, --color-surface, --font-body, --font-heading, --font-ui, --gap, --line-height, --loc-image-min, --loc-image-min-height, --loc-landscape-areas, --loc-landscape-columns, --loc-landscape-rows, --loc-narrow-areas, --loc-narrow-columns, --loc-narrow-rows, --loc-short-areas, --loc-short-columns, --loc-short-rows, --map-cone, --map-marker, --map-marker-route, --map-route, --page-max-width, --space-l, --space-m, --space-s, --space-xs, --target-size;
  • --app-areas and --app-rows arrange header, main and footer;
  • --loc-landscape-*, --loc-narrow-* and --loc-short-* arrange the location page (section 1.3);
  • --target-size and --loc-image-min-height can be raised; base.css keeps their lower limits (section 1.3).

docs.title: Narratives
docs.text:
[DRAFT – review] The assignment asks for two or three narratives, with the historical timeline required. The second one serves the use case of Bruno and Beatrix, who recreate shots.

data/narratives.json contains a list of 2 narratives. A narrative has: identifier, name, description (HTML, shown on the cover), lmml:estimatedMinutes, optionally lmml:orderedBy, and chapters. A chapter has: name, text (HTML, shown on the chapter page) and steps. A step has: locationId, lmml:transition (null on the first step of the narrative) and optionally lmml:texts.

The scripts turn a narrative into one sequence of screens: for each chapter, its chapter page, then one screen per step. Previous and next move along that sequence; the address of a chapter page is #/chapter/narrative/number and that of a step is the location page. A location can appear once in a narrative. The current narrative is chosen on the cover or with the switcher in the header, and is remembered.

Arrival times in sections 4.1 and 4.2 are computed from the data for a start at 9:00: the minutes of every transition, plus visitMinutesPerStop at every stop, with no break.

sections.title: Historical timeline
sections.text:
[DRAFT – review] The assignment states that “the order (and even the inclusion) of each location in the visit is totally dependent on the narrative proposed to the visitor”, and that visitors “are not simply strolling about the locations in a pseudo-random order, but move back and forward to follow a precise storytelling approach of the app” (Course slides, LMML project, A.Y. 2025-26, “Narratives”). The chapters are decades because the works cluster in distinct periods, from the 1960s to the 2010s, and each decade introduces a different way London was filmed.

The assignment states that “the order (and even the inclusion) of each location in the visit is totally dependent on the narrative proposed to the visitor” (Course slides, LMML project, A.Y. 2025-26, “Narratives”). York Rise was excluded because it was the costliest detour of the route. TODO (rewrite in my own words): The timeline follows the release year of the works, so its route crosses London several times instead of following the map: from Notting Hill to the City, back to Notting Hill and Mayfair, then to the river and up to Bloomsbury. This back-and-forth is intended. The same slide says that visitors “are not simply strolling about the locations in a pseudo-random order, but move back and forward to follow a precise storytelling approach of the app” (Course slides, LMML project, A.Y. 2025-26, “Narratives”). Only locations of the same year are ordered by distance (the two of 1964, the two of 1999, the four of 2003 and the two of 2010), which saves 25 minutes without breaking the chronology.

sections.title: Text selection algorithm
sections.text:
[DRAFT – review] Only some cells of the grid exist, so a switch moves to the closest existing text in the requested direction, and is disabled when there is none, so that a button never does nothing.

The functions are in js/textSelector.js and use no DOM and no stored state.

Texts considered. The texts of the location and those of the current narrative step are merged: a step text replaces the location text of the same cell and language. Texts with an invalid axis value are ignored. Only the texts in the current language are used; if there is none, all valid texts are used.

Preference. The visitor's preference is one value per axis, stored in the browser, initially medium · average · adult. It is kept from one location to the next.

First text of a page. The text with the smallest distance from the preference, the distance being the sum over the three axes of the difference in rank; ties go to the text nearest the centre of the grid (medium, average, adult).

A switch. Each of the six switches moves one step in one direction on one axis. The candidates are the texts strictly beyond the current one in that direction on that axis. Among them the choice is, in order: the smallest step on that axis; then the smallest distance from the preference on the other two axes; then the nearest to the centre. If there is no candidate the button is disabled. When a switch is used, the preference is updated on that axis only, to the value of the text reached, and in the narrow layout the content area is scrolled to the start of the text.

SwitchWording of the assignment (label in the wide layout, title attribute)Short label (narrow toolbar)Accessible name (aria-label)Move
moreTell me moreMoreMore: Tell me morelength +1
lessTell me lessLessLess: Tell me lesslength −1

With the texts that exist now (section 2.3), from medium · average · adult all six switches are enabled; on the short text Tell me less, Too difficult and Do you want to play? are disabled; on the long text Tell me more, Too simple and Additional details and references are disabled; in French all six are disabled.

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text:
[DRAFT – review] The site is static and must be published on GitHub Pages without a build step, and every part must be explainable at the exam. The course emphasises combining existing technologies (Leaflet, a QR library) rather than heavy tooling.

How the code is organised. Everything here describes the files as they are in the repository.

sections.text:

js/ contains 23 modules.

sections.title: Start-up and routing
sections.text:
js/app.js is the only script loaded by index.html. It runs, in order: load the three JSON files; check the data; restore the saved state; apply the theme; fill the two switchers and attach the listeners of header and footer; declare the routes and render the current one. If the data cannot be loaded, a message is shown in main.

The part of the address after # selects the view. js/router.js listens to the hashchange event. For each address it finds the matching route, calls the clean-up function returned by the previous view if there is one (the map and the location page return one), empties main, sets data-view on main to the page of the route, and calls the render function of the route; then the position in the narrative is remembered and header and footer are updated. An unknown address shows the 'Page not found' view.

AddressRoute namePageRender function
#/covercoverrenderCover
#/mapmapmaprenderMap
#/map/:idmap-focusmaprenderMap
#/location/:idlocationlocationrenderLocation

An address #/docs/3.2 opens the documentation scrolled to section 3.2; section numbers are computed from the position of each section in site.json.

sections.title: State
sections.text:
js/state.js keeps the visitor's choices in one object, saved in localStorage under the key lmml-state-v1. Reading and writing localStorage are protected, so the site works without it. Saved values are checked against the themes and narratives that exist now.

KeyContentInitial value
themeidentifier of the themedefaultTheme of site.json (victorian)
narrativeIdidentifier of the narrativedefaultNarrative of site.json (historical-timeline)
textPrefpreferred length, level and tonemedium, average, adult
lastPositionfor each narrative, index of the last screen visitedempty
activePanelpanel shown on a location page in the narrow layout: text, info or qrtext
langlanguage of the textsen

There is no automatic update: the code that changes the state also re-renders what depends on it.

sections.title: How themes and narratives are applied
sections.text:
Themes. The themes are listed in site.json (victorian, sixties). When the visitor picks one in the switcher, the state is saved, js/theme.js sets data-theme on the html element and changes the href of the theme stylesheet link, and the current view is rendered again.

Narratives. When the visitor picks a narrative in the switcher, or presses Start or Resume on the cover, the state is saved and the current view is rendered again. The narrative decides: the sequence followed by previous and next; the position shown between them; the transition, the chapter line and the step text of a location page; the route drawn on the map and the numbers of its markers.

Previous, next, return. On a location or chapter that belongs to the current narrative, previous and next follow the sequence; previous of the first screen is the cover. On a location or chapter that does not belong to it, previous and next are hidden and 'Return to the narrative' leads to the last screen visited in the narrative, or to its first screen. On the cover, next starts the narrative. Map, about, documentation, disclaimer and QR codes form a chain of their own and show 'Return to the narrative' once a narrative screen has been visited. The left and right arrow keys follow previous and next.

Map. js/render/map.js draws, for every location, a circle marker at geo, a view cone 45 metres long and 40 degrees wide from lmml:cameraPosition along lmml:cameraBearing, an arrow along the same direction and a dot at the camera position; and one dashed line through the steps of the current narrative in order. A marker opens the location page. #/map/identifier centres the map on one location.

QR codes. Each location page and the QR sheet draw a code that encodes baseUrl of site.json followed by #/location/identifier; if baseUrl is empty the address of the current page is used.

sections.title: Moving the controls into the toolbar on narrow screens
sections.text:
[DRAFT – review] CSS alone cannot move an element out of its parent, and the switches must sit in the bottom toolbar only on narrow screens.

js/render/location.js builds the text switches inside the text panel and the link 'Show on the map' inside the QR block. The article also contains an empty element, location-toolbar. The function placeControls(article, isNarrow) appends the element text-controls and the map link to the toolbar when isNarrow is true; when it is false it puts text-controls back as first child of the text panel and the map link as last child of the QR block. Moving an element keeps its listeners.

renderLocation creates a MediaQueryList with window.matchMedia for the query (orientation: portrait), (max-width: 600px), (max-height: 500px), calls placeControls once and again on every change event of that query, and returns a function that removes the listener; the router calls that function before rendering the next view.

The same query is written in css/base.css, section 11, where the toolbar and the tabs are displayed and laid out. The two must be changed together.

Checked on 2026-10-06 by resizing one page from 390×844 to 1280×800 and to 844×390: the switches and the link were in the toolbar, back in their panels, and in the toolbar again.
